title: The Spare Script
text:
Mira had signed up for the Riverside Players because the community theater needed people who could paint quickly and did not mind getting sawdust on their shoes. She had no role in the spring production. Most evenings, she worked behind the stage, labeling props, touching up scenery, and carrying chairs between scenes while the actors rehearsed under the bright work lights.

During the second week, one of the actors, Lena, began arriving late because her shift at a grocery store sometimes ran past six. No one treated it as a crisis. The director, Mr. Bell, simply adjusted the order of rehearsal when he could. Mira noticed the changes anyway. She kept a spare copy of the script on the paint table and began penciling in the entrances and exits for Lena's scenes. When she waited for one coat of paint to dry, she followed the dialogue with her finger. Once, when the stage was empty, she quietly spoke three of Lena's lines before returning to a half-finished doorway. She stopped when she heard footsteps in the hall.

A week later, Mr. Bell asked the crew to stay for a full run-through. Mira finished her work early, but instead of leaving, she pulled a folding chair to the back wall and watched. When Lena missed an entrance, Mira glanced down at the spare script before the stage manager called the scene to a stop. After rehearsal, Mira erased several old pencil marks and copied the new blocking notes into the margins. Her friend Tomas, who was stacking chairs nearby, asked why she bothered keeping the spare script so neat. Mira shrugged and said, "It helps me know what everyone needs."

On Thursday, rain hammered the theater roof as the cast arrived. Ten minutes before rehearsal, the stage manager read a message from Lena: a delivery truck had blocked the store's loading area, and Lena did not know when she would be able to leave work. Mr. Bell looked at the clock and then at the group gathering near the stage. "We can rehearse around her again," he began, "unless someone can read the part for the first two scenes."

Before he finished the sentence, Mira had closed the lid on a paint can and reached for the spare script, which was already open to the first scene. She did not raise her hand or step forward until Mr. Bell looked toward her. "You know the blocking?" he asked. Mira answered, "Most of it." She read the scenes with the cast. She missed one entrance and asked for a line once, but she moved to the correct side of the stage before the stage manager gave the usual cue.

Lena arrived halfway through rehearsal and thanked Mira before taking back the role. Mira returned to the scenery without mentioning the scenes again. Near the end of the evening, Mr. Bell stopped beside the paint table. He looked at the notes in the spare script, then at the black shoes Mira wore for crew work. "Bring those tomorrow," he said. "Just in case." Mira nodded once and tucked the script under the table instead of returning it to the supply shelf.

On her walk home, she passed the theater twice in her thoughts: first as it had looked from behind the scenery, and then as it had looked from the center of the stage. She still did not know whether Mr. Bell would need her again. But when she reached her apartment, she set an alarm fifteen minutes earlier than usual.
